title: universalcefr-check: a provenance and redundancy check over the public UniversalCEFR collection
description:
Applies a declare-then-test provenance check to the 24 public corpora of the UniversalCEFR collection: 13 languages, 65,037 rows. The method is to find the source a dataset declares, then test the data against that declaration rather than trusting it.

Much of the collection is sound: one schema across all 24 corpora, and the language field agrees with the corpus name on every row (a metadata-consistency check, not language identification). An exhaustive inversion of every normalised text onto the corpora holding it - no sampling, no threshold, no length floor - finds 131 texts present in more than one corpus. One is the single character "!", a degenerate row. The other 130 are a single pair.

That pair is cambridge_exams_en and elg_cefr_en, whose dataset cards declare different repositories, different papers and different licences. 130 of the 325 Cambridge texts are identical to an elg_cefr_en text after normalisation, and 324 of 325 match at 5-gram Jaccard 0.5 or better - one to one onto 324 distinct texts, median similarity 0.97, only 16 below 0.7 - with the CEFR labels agreeing on 324 of 324. Agreement between them is therefore not corroboration.

Two corpora repeat their own texts structurally under conflicting levels: cople2_pt (471 texts each present exactly twice, as A1/A2, B1/B2, C1/C2, with every other field verified identical) and elg_cefr_nl (1,195 texts stored as 3,596 rows, 1,190 of them three times). Ten corpora contain at least one such text, but only these two are structural; the 1.51x redundancy in caes_es is mostly short learner utterances genuinely coinciding and is not treated as a defect.

Two further findings concern declarations rather than duplication. The cefr_level field holds 17 distinct strings - the six bands, sub-band plus-levels in three corpora, a bare B, and four separate markers for no label. And the row-level license field disagrees with the dataset card in 13 of the 24 corpora; six differ substantively, and in three the rows state weaker terms than the card. One listed dataset, ComplexityMT, has no data files.

What the check cannot determine from outside is whether any of this originates upstream or in the conversion to the UniversalCEFR format; the two produce identical output. Every figure in the write-up is printed by the script. Redistributes no data - it downloads the published exports, and each corpus keeps its own licence.
